Veroia Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Veria, Greece

Demolished. Jews from Veroia are mentioned in the New Testament, dating presence to 49-50 CE; the 1453 Ottoman conquest expelled the community to Istanbul, though Spanish immigrants joined the remaining small Romaniot population in the first half of the 15th century. Population reached 737 by 1597, forming a cohesive, predominantly Sephardi community heavily influenced by nearby Salonika; the 17th-century Shabbatean movement led some to convert to Islam. An 18th-century synagogue was built (or extended) in Salonika's Sephardi style. Population fell to 149 by 1880, recovering to 500-600 by 1900 with new welfare organizations and an Alliance Israelite-supported school; refugees fleeing Salonika epidemics further boosted numbers. Zionist activity remained minimal in the 1920s. Population reached 850 before WWII; on March 31, 1943, 680 Jews were arrested and sent to Auschwitz via Salonika. About 130 survived, though only 2 families remained by the 1990s. This cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 15th century.
